## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

::: {.lx-lede}
[Lesson 0](00-grid-operator.qmd) ran one day like these hour by hour; [lesson 1](01-power-energy.qmd) showed that the area under a power curve is energy. Here the curve itself is the subject.
:::

```{=html}
<div id="t2-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>Daily shape</dt><dd>On 29 July 2025 demand rose from 298 MW at 04:00 to 450 MW at 16:00; on 21 January it had two humps, at 07:00 and 19:00.</dd>
<dt>Weekly rhythm</dt><dd>Weekend hours ran 4% below weekdays on average in 2025, and up to 9% lower around 07:00.</dd>
<dt>Seasons</dt><dd>July held the top hour; winter cold snaps made a second, lower season; April was the quietest month.</dd>
<dt>Load-duration curve</dt><dd>Sorted from highest to lowest, only 180 of 8,760 hours needed more than 90% of the peak.</dd>
<dt>Duck curve</dt><dd>Solar lowers midday net demand and steepens the evening climb that other plants must meet.</dd>
</dl>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>Load factor, and the area under the curve</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

The [load factor]{.lx-term term="load-factor"} is average demand over peak demand:

$$LF = \frac{\bar d}{d_{\max}} = \frac{282\ \text{MW}}{450\ \text{MW}} = 0.63 .$$

Sorting the hours changes their order, not their energy: $E = \sum_{h=1}^{8760} d_h \approx 2{,}469$ GWh either way. The share of the year's energy above a line $L$ is

$$\frac{\sum_h \max(0,\ d_h - L)}{E},$$

which for $L = 405$ MW is only 0.12%: the top tenth of the peak is a lot of capacity for very little energy. Screening studies compare plants against curves like this one; the Analyst tier (upcoming) builds one.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>Why planning models keep the hours in order</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

With a solar farm of $S$ MW whose output follows the shape $s_t$ (a share of its full output in hour $t$), net demand is

$$n_t = d_t - S\,s_t, \qquad \text{steepest climb} = \max_t \big(n_{t+3} - n_t\big).$$

The load-duration curve throws the time order away. That is fine for asking how many hours each MW is needed, but not for anything with memory: a battery's charge, a plant's ramp limit and the duck's evening neck all depend on which hour follows which. Planning models therefore run full chronological years, or a few representative days chained in order with the extreme days kept. The Modeler tier (upcoming) states those rules, and [lesson 9](index.qmd#lesson-9) (upcoming) lets storage fill the duck's belly.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper</span>What the data leave out</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li>One region only: the Southwest Power Pool in the central U.S., scaled down. Other regions peak at other hours and in other seasons.</li>
<li>For 699 hours of 2025 (about 8%) SPP's reported demand was implausible; those hours were rebuilt from SPP's own day-ahead forecast. The named days contain no rebuilt hours.</li>
<li>SPP has little solar (0.8% of its 2025 generation), so the duck curve adds a hypothetical farm that follows SPP's real solar shape.</li>
<li>Real net demand subtracts wind as well as solar; here only solar is subtracted, to isolate its effect.</li>
<li>One year of data cannot show long-term growth.</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
</div>
```
:::

## Check yourself
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="t2-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="noon" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Demand peaks at noon, when the sun is strongest.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. On 29 July 2025 the peak came at 16:00 to 17:00: buildings keep heating up after noon, and people come home.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="average" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Power plants are built for average demand.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. They must cover the peak hour, with a margin: Prairie Town averages 282 MW but peaks at 450 MW.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="evening" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Adding solar makes the evening easier for the other plants.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Solar fades while demand stays high, so the others must climb faster: on 30 May 2025, with 200 MW of solar, net demand rises 114 MW in three hours, against 20 MW without it.</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="t2">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="share" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">180 of the year's 8,760 hours need more than 405 MW. What share of the year is that?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">21%</li><li data-value="b">2.1%</li><li data-value="c">0.2%</li><li data-value="d">18%</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>2.1%: 180 ÷ 8,760 = 0.021. Capacity for those hours sits idle the other 98% of the year.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="heat" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">Which change would raise Prairie Town's winter morning peak the most?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">More solar panels</li><li data-value="b">Electric heat pumps replacing gas furnaces</li><li data-value="c">LED lighting everywhere</li><li data-value="d">A four-day work week</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Heat pumps: heating moves onto the grid on the coldest mornings, when demand already peaks. Solar does nothing before sunrise, and LEDs and fewer workdays lower demand.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
```
:::
